verdict: Neither framed option meets both hard requirements with confidence, so the either/or framing is wrong. Portcullis 5.2 alone fails R1. It does not proxy service-to-service traffic and offers mTLS only from the gateway to the first upstream (E2, E1). Lattice in sidecar mode fails R3 on the summed estimate from the internal mTLS STRICT measurement: 2.6 ms x 5 hops = 13 ms before any edge cost, and 13.8 ms with a 0.8 ms edge, against a 10 ms budget (E5, E1, K1, K2). That failure is likely but not proven. A sum of per-hop p99s equals the end-to-end p99 only when hops are fully correlated, and it usually overstates it when hops are independent with well-behaved tails (E13, E15, E18). This point is weaker than it looks, because E5's 'added p99 per hop' is probably a difference of p99s and not the p99 of the added delay, so those quantile results apply only loosely (E5, E18). The true end-to-end sidecar p99 could therefore be lower or higher. The best-supported choice this quarter is Lattice Service Mesh in node-proxy mode, with conditions. It has been GA since 3.2, and the platform team's note says it gives the same mTLS identity guarantees as sidecar mode (E6). It measured 0.9 ms per hop with mTLS STRICT, which sums to about 4.5 ms over 5 internal hops (E5, K4). In the recommended configuration Portcullis is not at the edge this quarter, so the edge is Lattice ingress or an existing edge, and its latency is unknown (E7). How much that edge may add depends on two unresolved readings: whether E5's 'per hop' counts one node proxy or two on a cross-node call (E5), and whether R3 means 5 or 6 proxied segments (E19). On the summed figure the edge may add up to 5.5 ms with one proxy per hop and 5 segments (K10), 4.6 ms with one proxy and 6 segments (K15, K16), and only 1.0 ms with two proxies and 5 segments (K12, K13). With two proxies and 6 segments the internal sum is 10.8 ms, which breaks R3 before any edge cost (K14). So the node-proxy pass on the summed figure is robust only under the one-proxy reading. The 5.3 ms total with a 0.8 ms Portcullis edge (K5) applies only to the later phased combination, under the one-proxy, 5-segment reading. Two conditions must be confirmed before committing. (a) The auditor must accept node-proxy mTLS, meaning per-workload certificates, rotation and STRICT enforcement. Today this rests only on an internal note (E6), supported by an Istio analogy (E10). (b) An end-to-end test of the full edge plus checkout chain must confirm R3. That test also settles the per-hop and segment-count readings in practice. The summed figure is not a guaranteed upper bound: rare per-hop spikes below 1% can compound across hops and push the end-to-end p99 above the sum (E14, E16, E18). Node-proxy Lattice does not cover R2. The only documented Lattice ingress feature is per-route rate limiting, with no per-tenant limits or API key auth (E4). Definition used throughout: 'one option' means one product the team adopts and runs this quarter. Lattice node-proxy and sidecar are modes of the same product. Portcullis plus in-app go-spiffe mTLS is not a single product. It also needs a SPIRE deployment (a Workload API server the team must run) plus code changes in all 14 services (E8), and no document says whether SPIRE counts against the one-option limit (E12). Ranked fallbacks, given that R1 has a hard audit date of 2027-06-30 while R2 has no stated deadline (E1): (1) Default: Lattice node-proxy now, and Portcullis at the edge in a later quarter for R2, if phasing is allowed (E12). (2) If the one-option limit is firm and R2 is wanted this quarter, still choose Lattice node-proxy and escalate the R2 gap, because R1 and R3 are hard and R2 is not. If R2 is made a hard requirement for this quarter, no single product in the packet covers R1, R2 and R3. The only Portcullis route that covers R1 adds SPIRE (E2, E8). Choose Portcullis plus go-spiffe/SPIRE only if stakeholders confirm SPIRE does not count as a second option. Otherwise the requirements conflict and must be escalated. The effort, latency and audit acceptance of this route are unquantified. (3) If the auditor rejects node-proxy, run the end-to-end test in sidecar mode. If sidecar's end-to-end p99 including the edge is at most 10 ms, choose Lattice sidecar. Otherwise choose Portcullis plus go-spiffe/SPIRE, subject to the same SPIRE confirmation. (4) If the decision is held strictly to the two options as stated, compare Lattice sidecar with the Portcullis option in both forms. Portcullis alone fails the hard R1 requirement outright (E2). Portcullis plus go-spiffe/SPIRE is admissible only if SPIRE does not count as a second option. Lattice sidecar likely fails R3 on the summed estimate (CL2), but that is not proven and can be tested before committing (E18). So do not adopt sidecar on the summed figures. Run the sidecar end-to-end test first. If it passes, choose Lattice sidecar: it enforces R1 centrally and meets R3 as measured. If it fails, the R3 breach is a measured violation of a hard limit. Portcullis plus go-spiffe/SPIRE fills R1 with in-app code whose risks are unquantified but not known failures, so choose it if SPIRE is allowed. If SPIRE is not allowed and sidecar fails, neither framed option meets both hard requirements. In that case the framing itself must be escalated, which is the case for node-proxy mode.

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Portcullis alone cannot meet R1. It covers only the gateway to the first upstream and does not proxy east-west traffic (E2). Lattice in either mode is the only option in the packet that provides mTLS on every hop as a platform feature. Node-proxy mode is documented internally as giving the same mTLS identity guarantees as sidecar mode (E6), but whether the audit will accept it is not established. Portcullis plus go-spiffe/SPIRE could provide east-west mTLS with rotating SVIDs (E8), but enforcement would depend on code in each service.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: A mesh moves mTLS into a proxy layer: a sidecar per pod, or a shared proxy per node. Identity issuance, rotation and STRICT enforcement are then set by central policy rather than by application code. A north-south gateway sits only on the edge path, so traffic between services never passes through it and gets no mTLS from it. A node-proxy mesh can still present per-workload identities if the shared proxy holds a separate certificate for each workload identity. Istio ztunnel does this (E10), but nothing shows Lattice does.
strengths: Lattice sidecar and node-proxy modes were both tested with mTLS STRICT on (E5)
Internal note says node-proxy gives the same mTLS identity guarantees as sidecar (E6)
go-spiffe streams updated X.509-SVIDs, so rotation in the in-app route needs no manual steps (E8)
weaknesses: Per-workload certificates in node-proxy mode are not confirmed for Lattice. E10 is only an analogy
Auditor criteria for mTLS evidence are not defined (E1 limitations)
The in-app route needs code changes in all 14 services plus running SPIRE, and its effort is not quantified (E8)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: On the summed per-hop estimate from the internal mTLS STRICT test, Lattice sidecar mode exceeds R3: 13 ms over 5 hops even with zero edge cost (K1), and 13.8 ms with a 0.8 ms edge (K2). For sidecar to fit on the sum, the per-hop cost would have to be at most 2 ms with no edge cost (K11), or at most 1.84 ms with a 0.8 ms edge (K8). The sum is exact under full correlation and usually overstates the end-to-end p99 for independent, well-behaved tails (E13, E15, E18). E5's per-hop figures are probably differences of p99s, though, so this applies only loosely (E5, E18). The sidecar failure is therefore likely but not proven, and it needs an end-to-end measurement. Node-proxy sums to 4.5 ms over 5 internal hops under the one-proxy-per-hop reading (K4). In the recommended this-quarter configuration the edge is not Portcullis and its latency is unknown (E7). The edge headroom depends on the combined per-hop and segment-count readings: 5.5 ms with one proxy and 5 segments (K10), 4.6 ms with one proxy and 6 segments (K16), 1.0 ms with two proxies and 5 segments (K13). With two proxies and 6 segments the internal sum is 10.8 ms, which fails R3 with zero edge cost (K14). With a 0.8 ms Portcullis edge (the phased combination, one-proxy 5-segment reading), the sum is 5.3 ms (K5). The node-proxy pass is also not proven: if per-hop delay has rare large spikes, the end-to-end p99 can exceed the sum (E14, E16, E18). The vendor's 0.4 ms (2 ms over 5 hops, K3) was measured with mTLS and telemetry off, so it does not apply to R1-compliant operation (E3).
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Each proxy adds handshake, encryption and decryption, L7 parsing and telemetry work on every hop. Larger payloads (6-40 KB against 1 KB) and higher rps (3,500 against 1,000) raise the per-hop cost (E3, E5). The internal sidecar figure is 6.5 times the vendor figure (K9). Sidecar mode puts proxies on both the client side and the server side of every hop. Node-proxy shares one proxy per node and does coarser L7 work (E6), which plausibly explains its lower cost. A cross-node call may still pass through two node proxies, and E5 does not say whether its 'per hop' figure covers one or both (E5). How per-hop p99s combine depends on the shape of the tails and on correlation (E18). (a) Fully correlated hops: the end-to-end p99 equals the sum (E13). (b) Independent hops with smooth tails: the end-to-end p99 is usually below the sum, so the sum is conservative (E15). (c) Independent hops with rare large spikes below 1% per hop: the spikes are invisible in each hop's p99 but compound across hops, so the end-to-end p99 can be well above the sum (E14, E16, E18). These results concern quantiles of the delays themselves. E5's 'added p99 per hop' is probably a difference of p99s (with mesh minus without), which is not the p99 of the added delay, so (a) to (c) apply to it only indirectly and the sum-is-conservative argument rests on weaker ground (E5, E18). K7 shows that across 5 independent hops only about 95.1% of requests avoid every hop's 1% tail. That measures how often a request meets at least one slow hop. It does not by itself show whether the sum overstates or understates the end-to-end p99. The packet's E14 and E15 disagree on how often case (c) matters in practice. Both are search-snippet sources and both can hold under different distributional conditions, so the disagreement cannot be settled for Lattice without per-hop histograms, which the packet does not have (E18). Node-proxy co-locates hops on shared proxies, which pushes it toward partial correlation, between cases (a) and (b) (E18).
strengths: The internal test matches R1 conditions (mTLS STRICT, telemetry on, checkout payloads) (E5)
Under the one-proxy, 5-segment reading, node-proxy's 4.5 ms internal sum leaves up to 5.5 ms for the edge (K4, K10)
weaknesses: No end-to-end edge plus checkout-chain measurement exists for any option, so neither the sidecar fail nor the node-proxy pass is proven (E7, E18)
The internal test reports no sample size, variance or repetitions, and does not say how 3,500 rps compares with production peak (E5)
Lattice ingress latency is unknown, and the Portcullis 0.8 ms edge figure is from 2 KB payloads (E2, E7)

If 'per hop' in E5 counts only one proxy, and a cross-node hop goes through two node proxies, the node-proxy internal sum is 9.0 ms over 5 segments (K12), leaving only 1.0 ms for whatever edge is used (K13)
R3 may mean 5 or 6 proxied segments (E19). Combined with the two-proxy reading, 6 segments give 10.8 ms internal, which breaks R3 before any edge cost (K14)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Portcullis meets R2 natively with API keys, OAuth2 and per-consumer and per-tenant rate limiting (E2). Lattice has documented per-route rate limiting at ingress only, with no mention of per-tenant limits or API key auth (E4). A Lattice-only choice therefore leaves R2 unmet or unproven. Public documentation is not available to settle this (E11).
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Per-tenant limiting needs the edge to identify the caller, for example from an API key, and to keep counters per tenant. Per-route limiting counts per path regardless of who calls, so it cannot enforce tenant quotas or authenticate keys.
strengths: Portcullis has native per-tenant limiting and API key auth (E2)
weaknesses: The only Lattice R2 evidence is the absence of a feature from a performance whitepaper, which does not prove the feature is missing (E4)
No product documentation can be found publicly (E11)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Portcullis alone is the lightest to run, but it does not solve R1. Adding the in-app go-spiffe route to it means changing code in 14 services and running SPIRE (E8). Lattice sidecar adds a proxy per pod for every service. Node-proxy shares one proxy per node, which should reduce injection and upgrade work, but the packet does not quantify this. Running both products later adds a second control surface for the same 3 engineers (E1).
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Operational load grows with the number of proxy instances, the number of code paths that handle certificates, and the number of products to upgrade and debug. A central mesh keeps certificate handling in one control plane. The in-app route spreads it across 14 codebases.
strengths: Node-proxy has fewer proxy instances than sidecar (E5, E6)
A gateway is a single component (E2)
weaknesses: No evidence quantifies operating effort for any option
Coarser L7 policies in node-proxy mode may push some policy work back into apps, and which policies are lost is not described (E6)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: R1 has a hard date of 2027-06-30 (E1). R2 has no stated deadline in requirements.md, which makes R2 the requirement that can be deferred more safely. Adopting the mesh in node-proxy mode now and Portcullis later fits the dates better than the reverse, because Portcullis first would leave R1 depending on an unquantified in-app build before the audit. The 'one option this quarter' limit comes only from the user's request, and whether phasing is allowed is unconfirmed (E12). If the limit is firm, the verdict's ranked fallbacks apply: Lattice node-proxy stays first unless R2 becomes a hard requirement for this quarter.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: The requirement with the compliance date and the broadest change (all 14 services) should start first, so there is time for rollout, STRICT enforcement and collecting audit evidence. The edge gateway is a single component that can be added later.
strengths: 'By Q2' in the request matches the 2027-06-30 audit date (E12, E1)
Nothing in the fixtures rules out adding the second product later (E12)
weaknesses: Phasing is not confirmed by any document (E12)
No date for R2 is given, so the business tolerance for deferring it is unknown (E1)

claims.text: Portcullis 5.2 alone cannot satisfy R1, because it does not proxy service-to-service traffic and offers mTLS only from the gateway to the first upstream.

On the summed per-hop estimate from the internal mTLS STRICT measurement, Lattice sidecar mode exceeds R3: 2.6 ms x 5 = 13 ms before the edge, and 13.8 ms with a 0.8 ms edge, both above 10 ms. The sum is exact only for fully correlated hops and usually overstates the end-to-end p99 for independent, well-behaved tails. Because E5's per-hop figures are probably differences of p99s, that result applies only loosely. The failure is likely but not proven until the end-to-end p99 is measured.

The vendor's 0.4 ms per-hop figure (2 ms over 5 hops) does not represent R1-compliant operation, because it was measured with mTLS and telemetry disabled at 1 KB payloads and 1,000 rps. The internal figure is 6.5 times higher.

On the summed approximation, Lattice node-proxy mode adds about 4.5 ms over 5 internal hops if E5's 'per hop' covers one node proxy. In the recommended this-quarter configuration the edge latency is unknown, and the edge headroom depends on two unresolved readings. It is 5.5 ms with one proxy and 5 segments, 4.6 ms with one proxy and 6 segments (internal 5.4 ms), and 1.0 ms with two proxies and 5 segments (internal 9.0 ms). With two proxies and 6 segments the internal sum is 10.8 ms, which fails R3 with zero edge cost. The 5.3 ms total and 4.7 ms headroom apply only if Portcullis (0.8 ms datasheet figure) is the edge, as in the later phased combination, under the one-proxy, 5-segment reading.

Summed per-hop p99s are not a guaranteed bound in either direction. They equal the end-to-end p99 for fully correlated hops, usually overstate it for independent hops with well-behaved tails, and can understate it when per-hop delay has rare large spikes that compound across hops. These quantile results apply only indirectly to E5, whose 'added p99 per hop' is probably a difference of p99s rather than the p99 of the added delay, so even the 'usually conservative' case is weakly supported here. Across 5 independent hops about 95.1% of requests avoid every hop's 1% tail, but that figure alone does not settle the direction. R3 must be confirmed for both sidecar and node-proxy modes by an end-to-end checkout-chain test.

Whether Lattice node-proxy mode meets the auditor's R1 requirements (per-workload certificates, rotation, STRICT enforcement) cannot be determined from the packet. Support is an internal note plus an analogy to Istio ambient mode.
Whether Lattice ingress supports per-tenant rate limiting and API key authentication cannot be determined. Only per-route rate limiting is documented, and no public documentation exists.
Portcullis natively meets R2 with API keys, OAuth2 and per-consumer and per-tenant rate limiting.

Portcullis combined with go-spiffe/SPIRE inside the 14 Go services could technically provide east-west mTLS with automatic SVID rotation. It is the only R1 path for a Portcullis-first choice. Its effort, latency and audit acceptability are not quantified.

Whether the one-option-this-quarter limit is firm, and whether the second product can be phased in later, cannot be determined from the documents. The limit comes only from the user's request. Whether a SPIRE deployment would count as a second option under that limit also cannot be determined.

R3 explicitly includes the edge, so the edge component's latency counts toward the 10 ms budget in addition to the internal hops. Whether R3 means 5 or 6 proxied segments is ambiguous in the fixtures. This analysis uses 5 as its base case, and a 6-segment reading adds one more per-hop increment to every sum. Combined with a two-node-proxy reading of E5, 6 segments put node-proxy at 10.8 ms internal, above R3 before any edge cost.
For sidecar mode to fit R3 on the summed estimate, per-hop added p99 would need to be at most 2 ms with zero edge cost, or at most 1.84 ms with a 0.8 ms edge. The measured 2.6 ms is above both.

alternatives.comparison: Fully meets R2 (E2) and adds only about 0.8 ms at the edge, but fails R1 because there is no east-west mTLS (E2). This option is not viable against the hard compliance requirement.

Provides mTLS on every hop, but the summed estimate of 13 ms over 5 hops already exceeds the 10 ms R3 budget before the edge (K1). The sum may be conservative, so an end-to-end test could still show a pass (E18). R2 is unproven, with only per-route limits documented (E4). This is the fallback if the auditor rejects node-proxy and an end-to-end test passes.

Expected to meet R1 if the audit accepts it (E6). It meets R3 on the summed estimate only if the unknown edge (Lattice ingress or an existing edge, E7) fits the remaining headroom. That headroom is 5.5 ms under the one-proxy, 5-segment reading (K4, K10), 4.6 ms with 6 segments (K16), and 1.0 ms with two proxies per hop (K13). There is none with two proxies and 6 segments (K14). R2 remains unmet or unproven (E4). It has fewer proxy instances to run than sidecar mode.

alternatives.option: Lattice node-proxy now, Portcullis at the edge in a later quarter
alternatives.comparison: Covers R1, R2 and R3 together at an estimated 5.3 ms summed, with 4.7 ms headroom under the one-proxy, 5-segment reading (K5, K6), but requires running two products with 3 engineers. Whether phasing is allowed is not confirmed (E12).

alternatives.option: Portcullis now plus in-app go-spiffe/SPIRE mTLS
alternatives.comparison: Meets R2 immediately and could meet R1 (E8). It is not a single product: it needs a SPIRE deployment the team must run plus code changes in all 14 services (E8), and whether SPIRE counts as a second option under the one-option limit is unconfirmed (E12). Its latency, effort and audit acceptance are all unquantified. That makes it a higher risk to the 2027-06-30 date than the mesh route. If SPIRE is confirmed not to count, it is the fallback when R2 is made hard this quarter, or when the auditor rejects node-proxy and sidecar fails an end-to-end test (including in the strict two-option case).

tradeoffs: Node-proxy has lower latency (0.9 against 2.6 ms per hop) but coarser L7 policy (E5, E6)
Choosing the mesh first protects the compliance date (R1), but leaves R2 tenant limits and API keys unaddressed until a gateway is added or Lattice ingress is confirmed (E1, E4)
Running both products covers every requirement but roughly doubles the operating surface for 3 engineers (E1)
The in-app mTLS route avoids a mesh, but spreads certificate and enforcement logic across 14 codebases (E8)
edgeCasesAndFailureModes: If E5's 'per hop' counts one proxy and cross-node calls go through two node proxies, the node-proxy internal sum is 9.0 ms over 5 segments (K12). That leaves only 1.0 ms for whatever edge is used (K13)

The edge in the recommended configuration (Lattice ingress or an existing edge) has unknown latency (E7). For node-proxy to fit on the sum, it must stay at or below 5.5 ms under the most favourable reading (K10), 4.6 ms with 6 segments (K16), and 1.0 ms with two proxies per hop (K13). Portcullis latency at 6-40 KB payloads may also be above its 2 KB datasheet figure of 0.8 ms (E2)

Correlation between hops does not by itself make the end-to-end p99 worse than the sum. Full correlation makes the two equal (E13). Rare large per-hop spikes below 1% can push the end-to-end p99 above the sum (E14, E16, E18). Node-proxy's shared per-node proxy makes hops partially correlated (E18). Conversely, smooth independent tails could put sidecar's true end-to-end p99 below its 13 ms sum (E15, E18)
Production peak rps above the tested 3,500 could raise per-hop cost (E5)
If node-proxy certificates are per node rather than per workload, the auditor may reject it for R1 (E6, E10)
If tenant limits are needed before a gateway is added, a mesh-only interim leaves tenants without quotas (E4)

If R3 is read as 6 proxied segments, every summed total rises by one more per-hop increment: node-proxy becomes 5.4 ms internal with one proxy per hop (K15). Combined with the two-proxy reading it becomes 10.8 ms, which breaks R3 before any edge cost (K14, E19)

counterarguments.argument: The vendor benchmark shows 0.4 ms per hop, so sidecar latency is fine.
counterarguments.response: That benchmark disabled mTLS and telemetry and used 1 KB at 1,000 rps (E3). R1 requires mTLS, and the internal STRICT test at checkout payloads measured 2.6 ms (E5), giving a summed 13 ms over 5 hops (K1). The internal test is more representative because it runs the required configuration (mTLS STRICT, telemetry on) on the team's own checkout payloads.

counterarguments.argument: The internal test may be unreliable, since it reports no sample size or variance, and summed p99s may overstate the end-to-end figure.
counterarguments.response: Both points are valid (E5 limitations, E15, E18). With no reported variance, the packet cannot say how likely a measurement error is that would close the gap between 2.6 ms and the 1.84-2 ms per-hop thresholds (K8, K11). The summed estimate is usually conservative for well-behaved independent tails, so sidecar could pass end to end. That argument is weaker here than in the general case: E5's 'added p99 per hop' is probably a difference of p99s, not the p99 of the added delay, so the quantile-additivity results (E13-E15) do not apply directly (E5, E18). This is why the sidecar failure is stated as likely, not proven, and why the end-to-end test should cover sidecar mode as well as node-proxy. Node-proxy is preferred because its summed estimate is within budget under the one-proxy reading, not because sidecar's failure is certain.

counterarguments.argument: Node-proxy mode is not one of the two options on the table.
counterarguments.response: The decision objective explicitly asks whether node-proxy mode fits better. It is the same product (Lattice 3.x, GA since 3.2) (E6), so adopting it does not add a third vendor. If the two-option framing is held strictly, fallback (4) applies. Portcullis alone fails R1 outright (E2), so the comparison is Lattice sidecar, subject to an end-to-end R3 test, against Portcullis plus go-spiffe/SPIRE if SPIRE is allowed (E8, E12).

counterarguments.argument: Portcullis plus go-spiffe solves R1 without a mesh.
counterarguments.response: It is technically feasible (E8), but it costs code changes in 14 services plus running SPIRE, has unquantified latency, and relies on each service enforcing STRICT. That is a heavier and riskier path for a 3-engineer team against a fixed audit date. It is also not a single product, because SPIRE is a second component whose status under the one-option limit is unconfirmed (E8, E12). It remains the fallback if R2 must land this quarter, or if sidecar fails an end-to-end test, but only if SPIRE is confirmed not to count as a second option.
